title: Migraine After Drinking: Why Alcohol Triggers Attacks and What Helps
excerpt: Can alcohol cause migraines? Why drinking triggers attacks in some people, why red wine is the usual suspect, how to tell a migraine from a hangover, and what you can safely take.
metaDescription: Why alcohol triggers migraines, which drinks are worst, how to tell a migraine from a hangover, what to take safely, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, alcohol is a real migraine trigger for some people, but not for everyone with migraine, and not every time. When it does trigger an attack, the drink type often matters as much as the amount. Red wine is the drink people with migraine name most often, while clear spirits seem to cause trouble less often. The attack can start within a few hours of drinking or show up the next morning, and that second kind is easy to confuse with an ordinary hangover. This guide explains how alcohol sets off migraines, how to tell a migraine apart from a hangover headache, what you can take safely, and which patterns mean you should talk to a doctor.

**The quick rules:** If drinking reliably gives you migraines, keep a simple log for a month (drink type, amount, food, sleep, stress, and when the headache started) so you know your real trigger instead of guessing. Try clear spirits in small amounts rather than red wine, drink water alongside every drink, eat before and while drinking, and protect your sleep. Treat an attack early with whatever your doctor has advised, and never take painkillers before bed "just in case." If you get a sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst of your life, or a headache with weakness, numbness, confusion, slurred speech, or vision loss, treat it as an emergency, not a hangover.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research. It is not medical advice and doesn't replace a doctor who knows your history. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if you have a sudden, explosive headache that peaks within about a minute, the worst headache of your life, a headache with a stiff neck and fever, weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, confusion, fainting, a seizure, or a headache after hitting your head while drinking. **Book a regular appointment** if your migraines are new, are getting more frequent, change in pattern, start after age 50, come with aura for the first time, or if you are taking pain relievers on more than a few days a week. If you drink heavily most days and get headaches with shaking, sweating, or a racing heart when you cut back, those can be withdrawal signs. Tell a doctor plainly, because stopping suddenly after long heavy use can be dangerous and is safer with medical help.

## Can Alcohol Cause Migraines? What the Research Says

Doctors who study headaches treat alcohol as a recognized migraine trigger. The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3), the reference system neurologists use to define headache types, includes a category called "alcohol-induced headache." It has two forms, which line up with what many drinkers notice:

- **Immediate alcohol-induced headache** starts within about three hours of drinking. People with migraine are more prone to this kind, and it can happen after a fairly small amount.
- **Delayed alcohol-induced headache** starts roughly 5 to 12 hours later, after blood alcohol has fallen. This is the one most people call a hangover headache, and in people with migraine it often looks and behaves like a migraine attack.

Surveys of people with migraine consistently find that a sizable minority name alcohol as a trigger. A Dutch survey of more than 2,000 migraine patients, published in the *European Journal of Neurology* in 2019, found that roughly a third reported alcohol as a trigger, and red wine was by far the most commonly named drink. The same survey also found that many people with migraine drink less than the general population, or avoid alcohol altogether, partly because of their headaches.

There's an important catch. Reported triggers aren't always reliable triggers. In that survey and others, many people who blamed alcohol said it set off an attack only some of the time. Migraine triggers tend to add up: a glass of wine on a well-rested, well-fed, calm evening may do nothing, while the same glass after a short night's sleep, a skipped lunch, and a stressful week tips you over the edge. That's why a simple trigger diary is more useful than a blanket rule.

## Why Alcohol Triggers Migraines: The Likely Mechanisms

Nobody has pinned down a single cause. Researchers have several reasonable explanations, and more than one may be at work in the same person.

### 1. Alcohol widens blood vessels and affects pain signaling

Alcohol relaxes blood vessels, which is part of why your face may flush when you drink. Older theories blamed migraine mainly on swelling blood vessels in the head. Today, migraine is understood as a brain and nerve disorder first, with blood vessel changes as part of the picture rather than the whole story. Still, alcohol acts on several systems that matter in migraine, including the trigeminal nerve (the main pain nerve of the face and head), serotonin signaling, and inflammation. In a brain that's already prone to migraine, those nudges may be enough to start an attack.

### 2. The by-products of breaking down alcohol

Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde and then into acetate. Acetaldehyde is the toxic compound behind facial flushing and some hangover symptoms. A 2010 study in rats, published in *PLoS ONE*, suggested that acetate itself may contribute to the delayed headache that follows drinking. That's an animal finding, so it's a clue rather than proof, but it fits with the fact that many alcohol headaches arrive once the alcohol is mostly gone.

### 3. Other compounds in the drink (congeners)

Alcoholic drinks contain more than ethanol. Congeners are the extra compounds made during fermentation and aging, and they give darker drinks much of their color and flavor. Red wine, whiskey, brandy, and dark rum have more of them. Vodka and gin have very little. Congeners are linked to worse hangovers in general, and several of them are suspects in migraine:

- **Histamine.** Red wine contains more histamine than white wine. Some people break down histamine more slowly, and alcohol can make that slower still. Histamine can cause headaches, flushing, and a stuffy nose.
- **Tyramine.** This compound is found in aged and fermented foods and some drinks, including some tap beers and certain wines. It has long been suspected as a migraine trigger, although the evidence is mixed.
- **Phenolic compounds and flavonoids.** Red wine is rich in these plant compounds, which come from grape skins. Some researchers think they may affect serotonin release in a way that matters for migraine.

Our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains which drinks contain the most.

### 4. Dehydration, poor sleep, and missed meals

Alcohol makes you urinate more, so a night of drinking can leave you mildly dehydrated. It also breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night, even if it helps you fall asleep. People often eat irregularly or skip breakfast after a night out. Dehydration, poor sleep, and low blood sugar are all well-known migraine triggers on their own. Alcohol often brings all three at once, which helps explain why a migraine after drinking can feel worse than one from a single trigger.

### 5. Sugar, mixers, and caffeine

Sweet cocktails, energy drink mixers, and coffee-based drinks add their own variables. Caffeine is a tricky one for people with migraine. A modest amount can help some attacks, but heavy daily use and then a sudden drop can cause rebound headaches. Mixing alcohol with energy drinks also tends to make people drink more than they notice. See our guide to [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol) for more on that combination.

## Red Wine and Migraines: Why It's the Usual Suspect

Red wine shows up again and again in migraine research and patient surveys. A small, often-cited study published in *The Lancet* in 1988 compared red wine with vodka in people who believed red wine triggered their migraines. The red wine set off attacks in a number of them, while vodka mixed to the same alcohol content did not. That was a small study and doesn't settle the question, but it supports the idea that something in red wine beyond the alcohol itself is often to blame.

Sulfites get a lot of the blame, but they're probably not the main culprit. White wine usually contains as much or more sulfite than red wine, yet red wine is the bigger headache trigger for most people. Sulfites mainly cause breathing problems in a small group of sensitive people, especially some with asthma. Histamine, tannins, and other phenolic compounds are more likely explanations for red-wine headaches. We cover this in more detail in [red wine headache](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) and [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

If red wine is your trigger, it's worth testing whether white wine, a lighter red, or a clear spirit behaves differently for you. Many people find they tolerate some drinks well and others badly.

## Which Drinks Are Most and Least Likely to Trigger a Migraine?

There's no drink that's guaranteed safe, and individual reactions vary a lot. Based on what the research and patient surveys suggest, here's a rough guide.

| Drink | General pattern for people with migraine |
|---|---|
| Red wine | Most commonly reported trigger. High in histamine, tannins, and phenolic compounds. |
| Dark spirits (whiskey, brandy, dark rum) | Higher in congeners. Often reported as worse for hangovers and headaches. |
| Beer and cider | Mixed. Some people react, possibly to tyramine, histamine, or the volume of fluid and alcohol consumed. |
| Sparkling wine and champagne | Bubbles speed up alcohol absorption, which may bring on an immediate headache faster for some people. |
| White wine | Reported as a trigger less often than red, though still a problem for some. |
| Clear spirits (vodka, gin) with a non-sugary mixer | Lowest in congeners. Reported as a trigger least often, but the alcohol itself can still trigger an attack. |

Two points matter more than the drink type:

1. **Amount.** The more you drink, the more likely you are to get a delayed headache, whether you have migraine or not.
2. **Speed.** Drinking quickly raises blood alcohol fast, which seems to matter for immediate headaches in sensitive people.

## Migraine vs. Hangover Headache: How to Tell the Difference

A migraine after drinking and a hangover headache can overlap, especially the morning after. Some signs point more toward migraine.

| Feature | Typical hangover headache | Typical migraine |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Usually both sides, across the forehead or whole head | Often one side, though it can be both |
| Feel | Dull, pressing, throbbing that gets worse with movement | Pulsing or throbbing, moderate to severe |
| Other symptoms | Thirst, tiredness, nausea, shakiness, poor concentration | Sensitivity to light and sound, nausea or vomiting, sometimes aura |
| Aura | No | Sometimes: zigzag lines, blind spots, flashing lights, tingling, usually before the pain |
| Timing | Next morning, fades as the day goes on | Can start within hours of drinking or the next day; may last 4 to 72 hours |
| Effect of rest in a dark room | Helps a bit | Often essential |
| Your history | Anyone can get one | You usually have migraines from other triggers too |

If you already have a migraine diagnosis and your "hangover" after one or two drinks feels like your usual migraine (one-sided, light-sensitive, nauseous), it's probably a migraine and should be treated like one. If you've never had migraines and only get dull headaches after heavy drinking, it's more likely a standard hangover. Our article on [why alcohol causes headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025) covers the ordinary hangover headache in more depth.

### Cluster headaches are a special case

Cluster headache is a different, rarer disorder: one-sided pain around the eye that is extremely severe, often with a watery eye and runny nostril on the same side. During an active cluster period, alcohol is one of the most reliable triggers, sometimes within an hour of a single drink. Many people with cluster headache avoid alcohol completely during a cluster. If this description fits you, see a doctor. Cluster headaches respond to specific treatments that differ from migraine care.

## What to Take for a Migraine After Drinking

If you have migraine, the best plan is the one you've already worked out with your doctor. Here's how the common options fit with alcohol. Always check labels and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

### Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin (NSAIDs)

These are a common first choice for migraine. They're easier on the liver than acetaminophen, but harder on the stomach. Alcohol already irritates the stomach lining, and the labels warn about a higher risk of stomach bleeding for people who have three or more drinks a day. If you take one after drinking, eat something first, drink water, and stick to the label dose. People with ulcers, kidney disease, or heart disease, or who take blood thinners, should ask a pharmacist first. More detail is in our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).

### Acetaminophen (Tylenol)

It's gentler on the stomach, but the liver processes it, and heavy regular drinking increases the risk of liver injury. A single normal dose once the alcohol has cleared is usually reasonable for a healthy person who doesn't drink heavily day to day. Count acetaminophen from every product, including cold and flu medicines. See [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for the details.

### Excedrin and other combination pills

Excedrin Migraine combines acetaminophen, aspirin, and caffeine. That means you get both the liver concern and the stomach concern, plus caffeine on top of whatever caffeine you had while drinking. Our [Excedrin and alcohol](/never-hungover/excedrin-and-alcohol) guide walks through the trade-offs.

### Triptans (sumatriptan, rizatriptan, and others)

Triptans are prescription migraine drugs that work on serotonin receptors to stop an attack. There's no well-known dangerous chemical interaction between triptans and a moderate amount of alcohol, but both can cause dizziness and drowsiness, and alcohol can make your migraine harder to treat. Many doctors suggest waiting until you've sobered up before taking one, and not drinking more after you do. Ask your prescriber what they recommend for you.

### Gepants and other newer migraine drugs

Newer medicines such as the CGRP-blocking pills used to treat or prevent migraine don't have a well-known direct interaction with alcohol. But alcohol can still trigger attacks that work against your treatment. If you take a daily preventive medicine, such as topiramate, amitriptyline, or a beta blocker, ask your doctor about alcohol specifically. Some of these add to alcohol's sedating effects.

### A few things to avoid

- **Don't take painkillers before bed "to stay ahead of it."** You'd be adding medicine while your body is still processing alcohol, often on an empty stomach, before you know you need it.
- **Don't take more than the label says.** Extra tablets won't stop a migraine faster, and they add risk.
- **Watch how often you're taking pain relievers.** Using them on many days a month can cause medication overuse headache, where the pills themselves keep the headaches going. If you're reaching for them more than a couple of days a week, talk to a doctor.
- **If you take an MAOI antidepressant,** ask your doctor about alcohol. Some tap beers and aged or fermented drinks contain tyramine, which can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure with these drugs.

## Self-Care During an Alcohol-Triggered Migraine

Medication isn't the only thing that helps. While you wait for it to work, or if you'd rather not take more:

- **Drink water or an electrolyte drink in small, steady sips.** If you're nauseous, sipping works better than gulping.
- **Lie down in a dark, quiet room.** Light and sound sensitivity are central migraine features, and reducing them helps.
- **Use a cold pack on your forehead or the back of your neck.** Many people find cold soothing during a migraine.
- **Eat something plain once you can.** Toast, crackers, or a banana can help steady blood sugar.
- **Use caffeine with care.** A small amount of coffee helps some people's migraines, especially if they drink coffee every day and are due their usual cup. Too much can make nausea and dehydration worse.
- **Sleep it off if you can.** For many people, sleep is what ends a migraine.

Our article on [fast hangover headache relief](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) covers more practical options for the morning after.

## How to Drink Without Triggering a Migraine

If you have migraine and want to keep drinking socially, these steps give you the best odds. None of them is a guarantee.

1. **Know your personal trigger.** Keep a log for a month or two. Write down the drink, how much, how fast, what you ate, how much you slept the night before, your stress level, and for women, where you are in your cycle. Patterns often appear quickly.
2. **Pick your drink deliberately.** If red wine is a problem, try a small amount of a clear spirit with soda water, or a white wine. Test one change at a time.
3. **Set a limit before you start.** For many people with migraine, the threshold is low, sometimes one or two drinks. Decide in advance and stick to it.
4. **Slow down.** Make each drink last, and alternate every alcoholic drink with a glass of water.
5. **Eat a proper meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood and helps keep your blood sugar steady.
6. **Avoid stacking triggers.** If you're already short on sleep, stressed, hungry, or close to your period, it may be a bad night to drink.
7. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed, and try to keep your usual wake-up time.
8. **Skip drinking during a bad patch.** If your migraines are frequent right now, alcohol is more likely to push you over the edge.

For broader advice on hangover prevention, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When Alcohol and Migraine Need a Closer Look

Some patterns are worth raising with a doctor, even if each headache seems manageable on its own:

- **You get a migraine after very small amounts of alcohol** and it's getting worse over time.
- **You get flushing, hives, a stuffy nose, or a racing heart along with the headache.** That may point to alcohol intolerance or a histamine reaction rather than migraine alone. Our [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) guide explains the difference.
- **Your headaches have changed character** (new location, new type of pain, aura you've never had before).
- **You're taking pain relievers on many days a month.**
- **You're using alcohol to cope with migraine pain.** Alcohol can feel like it takes the edge off, but it tends to make migraines worse overall and interacts with many migraine medicines.

A doctor can help confirm the diagnosis, check for other causes, and talk about preventive treatment if attacks are frequent. Modern migraine care has more options than it did a decade ago.

## Where Do Hangover Supplements Fit?

People with migraine sometimes ask whether hangover supplements can help. The honest answer is that there is no good evidence that any hangover supplement prevents or treats alcohol-triggered migraines. Migraine is a brain disorder with its own triggers and treatments, and a supplement isn't a substitute for a migraine plan from your doctor.

Some people do use supplements to feel better after a night out more generally:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. There's no research showing it prevents migraines. If you want to try it for general hangover symptoms, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription migraine drugs, check with your doctor or pharmacist first.
- **Magnesium and riboflavin (vitamin B2)** have some evidence as daily migraine preventives in general, separate from drinking. These are worth discussing with your doctor if you have frequent migraines, rather than taking them only on drinking nights.

The step with the clearest benefit is still the simplest: for many people with migraine, drinking less, choosing drinks carefully, and protecting sleep and meals does more than any supplement.

If your pain starts within an hour of a single drink and you don't have a migraine history, the mechanisms are often different; our guide to [a headache after just one drink](/never-hungover/headache-after-one-drink) covers those fast-onset causes.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol is a recognized migraine trigger, but it affects some people with migraine and not others, and often only when other triggers stack up.
- Attacks can start within about three hours of drinking or the next morning, and the morning-after version is easy to mistake for a hangover.
- Red wine is the drink most often blamed. Clear spirits in small amounts are reported as a trigger least often.
- Treat an attack with the plan your doctor has given you. Be careful with painkillers after drinking: NSAIDs are hard on the stomach and acetaminophen on the liver. Don't take either before bed as prevention.
- A trigger diary is the most useful tool you have.
- A sudden, severe headache or a headache with neurological symptoms is an emergency, whether or not you've been drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can alcohol cause migraines?**

Yes, for some people. Alcohol is a recognized migraine trigger, and surveys of people with migraine find that roughly a third report it as a trigger, with red wine named most often. It doesn't trigger attacks in everyone with migraine, and many people find it only does so some of the time, usually when other triggers such as poor sleep, stress, or skipped meals are also present.

**Why do I get a migraine after just one drink?**

Some people with migraine are sensitive to small amounts of alcohol, especially red wine. The likely reasons include alcohol's effects on blood vessels and pain nerves, and compounds in certain drinks such as histamine, tyramine, and phenolic compounds. Doctors recognize an "immediate" alcohol headache that can start within about three hours of drinking. If it's new, getting worse, or comes with flushing, hives, or a racing heart, talk to a doctor, because it could also be alcohol intolerance.

**How long does a migraine after drinking last?**

A migraine typically lasts anywhere from 4 to 72 hours if it isn't treated. Alcohol-triggered headaches usually clear within 72 hours. Treating the attack early with the plan your doctor has given you, resting in a dark room, and rehydrating usually shortens it. A headache that lasts longer than three days, or keeps getting worse, should be checked by a doctor.

**Is it a migraine or a hangover?**

Migraines are more often one-sided and pulsing, and they come with sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, and sometimes aura (visual changes such as zigzag lines before the pain starts). Hangover headaches are usually dull, on both sides, and come with thirst, tiredness, and shakiness. If you already have migraines and your headache after drinking feels like your usual attack, treat it as a migraine.

**What alcohol is least likely to trigger a migraine?**

Clear spirits such as vodka or gin, in small amounts and with a non-sugary mixer, are reported as a trigger least often, because they're low in congeners. Red wine is reported most often. That said, the alcohol itself can still trigger a migraine in sensitive people, and reactions vary a lot, so testing one drink at a time is the best way to learn your own pattern.

**Can I take a triptan if I've been drinking?**

There's no well-known dangerous interaction between triptans such as sumatriptan and a moderate amount of alcohol, but both can cause dizziness and drowsiness. Many doctors suggest waiting until you've sobered up before taking one and not drinking more afterward. Ask your prescriber for advice specific to you, especially if you also take other medicines.

**Does red wine cause migraines because of sulfites?**

Probably not, in most cases. White wine often contains as much or more sulfite than red, yet red wine is the bigger migraine trigger. Researchers suspect histamine, tannins, and other phenolic compounds from grape skins instead. Sulfites mainly cause breathing problems in a small group of sensitive people, particularly some with asthma.

**When should I see a doctor about migraines after drinking?**

Go to the emergency room for a sudden, severe headache that peaks within about a minute, the worst headache of your life, or a headache with weakness, numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, a stiff neck with fever, or a seizure. Book a regular appointment if your migraines are new, getting more frequent, changing in pattern, starting after age 50, or if you're taking pain relievers on many days each month.
